questions.stem: Which observation shows that a sessile organism can still produce movement?

options.text: A plant shoot grows toward a light source
options.why: The plant remains rooted, but part of it changes position through directional growth. Movement doesn’t require locomotion.

options.text: A whale swims between its feeding and breeding grounds
options.why: That’s migration by a motile animal. It doesn’t show movement in an organism fixed in one location.

options.text: A gazelle runs away when it detects a predator
options.why: That’s locomotion used to escape danger. The gazelle changes its whole-body location.

options.text: A moth flies toward the pheromones released by a mate
options.why: That’s locomotion used to find a mate. The example involves a freely moving animal.

questions.stem: Which change occurs when a sarcomere contracts?

options.text: The A band shortens as the myosin filaments contract
options.why: The A band marks the length of the thick filaments, which stays constant. Myosin filaments don’t shorten.

options.text: The Z lines move closer while the I band narrows
options.why: Actin slides farther over myosin, bringing the Z lines closer and reducing the actin-only region.

options.text: The actin filaments shorten while the H zone stays constant
options.why: Actin keeps the same length, and the H zone narrows as thin filaments move farther toward the center.

options.text: The Z lines move apart while filament overlap increases
options.why: Increased overlap shortens the sarcomere, so its Z lines move closer rather than farther apart.

questions.stem: What directly exposes the myosin-binding sites on actin?

options.text: ATP binds to actin and removes troponin
options.why: ATP binds to myosin during the cross-bridge cycle. Troponin remains present and responds to calcium.

options.text: Calcium binds to troponin, shifting tropomyosin
options.why: The shape change in troponin moves tropomyosin away from the binding sites on actin.

options.text: Myosin hydrolyzes calcium and releases phosphate
options.why: Myosin hydrolyzes ATP, not calcium. Calcium acts as a signal by binding to troponin.

options.text: Titin pulls tropomyosin away from the actin filament
options.why: Titin aids elastic recoil and limits stretching. It doesn’t regulate actin’s binding sites.

questions.stem: What is the role of ATP after a myosin head has completed a power stroke?

options.text: ATP binds to myosin and causes detachment from actin
options.why: Binding of a new ATP molecule breaks the cross-bridge. Its later hydrolysis re-energizes the myosin head.

options.text: ATP binds to actin and shortens the thin filament
options.why: Thin filaments keep the same length. ATP acts through myosin rather than shortening actin.

options.text: ATP binds to troponin and exposes the active sites
options.why: Calcium binds to troponin to expose the sites. ATP has a different role in the myosin cycle.

options.text: ATP binds to titin and stretches the whole sarcomere
options.why: Titin is stretched by opposing forces and stores elastic energy. ATP doesn’t drive that stretching.

questions.stem: Which description defines a motor unit?

options.text: One motor neuron and every muscle fibre it controls
options.why: Branches of one motor neuron form neuromuscular junctions with all the fibres belonging to its motor unit.

options.text: One sensory neuron and all receptors connected to it
options.why: That describes sensory input rather than motor control. A motor unit contains a motor neuron and muscle fibres.

options.text: One muscle fibre and all motor neurons reaching it
options.why: The relationship is backwards. A motor unit is organized around one motor neuron, which may control many fibres.

options.text: One muscle and every tendon attached across its joint
options.why: Tendons transmit muscle force to bones. They aren’t components of a motor unit.

questions.stem: How can the nervous system increase the force produced by a skeletal muscle?

options.text: By recruiting additional motor units
options.why: Recruitment activates more muscle fibres, so their combined contraction produces greater force.

options.text: By lengthening each myosin filament
options.why: Myosin filament length stays constant. Force changes through activation patterns, including motor-unit recruitment.

options.text: By converting tendons into contractile tissue
options.why: Tendons transmit force but don’t contract. Muscle fibres are the contractile cells.

options.text: By filling the joint cavity with more cartilage
options.why: Cartilage reduces friction and absorbs compression. It doesn’t control how many fibres contract.

questions.stem: Why are antagonistic muscles required to reverse a skeletal movement?

options.text: A muscle produces force by contracting and cannot actively push itself longer
options.why: The opposing muscle must contract to pull the bones in the reverse direction while the first muscle lengthens.

options.text: A muscle can push effectively but cannot pull on a tendon
options.why: Muscles do the opposite: they pull through tendons when they contract and don’t push bones apart.

options.text: Both muscles must contract equally to move a joint
options.why: Equal opposing forces would resist movement. For a movement, the agonist contracts while its antagonist lengthens.

options.text: Ligaments contract to return each muscle to its resting length
options.why: Ligaments stabilize joints and aren’t contractile. Opposing muscles and titin contribute to return movement.

questions.stem: Which structure connects bone to bone and limits excessive movement at a synovial joint?

options.text: Tendon
options.why: A tendon joins muscle to bone and transmits the force of contraction.

options.text: Ligament
options.why: A ligament joins bone to bone, stabilizing the joint and restricting unsafe movement.

options.text: Cartilage
options.why: Cartilage covers articulating surfaces, reducing friction and absorbing compression.

options.text: Synovial fluid
options.why: Synovial fluid lubricates the joint cavity. It doesn’t connect the bones.

questions.stem: What is the best method for comparing a hip joint’s range of motion in different dimensions?

options.text: Measure joint angles for several movements using consistent anatomical landmarks
options.why: A goniometer or image analysis can measure the angle through which the joint moves in each plane.

options.text: Count the motor units present in each muscle around the hip
options.why: Motor-unit number affects control and force, not the angle through which the joint can move.

options.text: Measure the length of the femur in each movement plane
options.why: The femur’s length doesn’t change. Range of motion is measured as an angle at the joint.

options.text: Record the volume of synovial fluid after each movement
options.why: Synovial fluid provides lubrication, but its volume isn’t a measure of the joint’s movement angle.

options.text: External intercostals contract and lift the ribs up and out
options.why: That action helps inspiration. It increases thoracic volume rather than aiding forced expiration.

options.text: Internal intercostals contract and move the ribs down and in
options.why: Their fibre orientation lets them pull the ribcage opposite to the external intercostals during forced expiration.

options.text: Both intercostal layers relax while the ribs rise
options.why: Rising ribs increase thoracic volume. Forced expiration uses active contraction of the internal intercostals.

options.text: Titin contracts actively and pulls the ribcage downward
options.why: Titin recoils elastically rather than contracting as a motor protein. Muscle fibres generate the active force.

questions.stem: Which example pairs a reason for locomotion with an appropriate behavior?

options.text: Migration: a whale travels between feeding and breeding grounds
options.why: Migration is sustained movement between regions, often linked to seasonal feeding or reproduction.

options.text: Escape: a cheetah runs toward prey during a hunt
options.why: The cheetah is foraging for food. Escape locomotion moves an organism away from danger.

options.text: Finding a mate: a gazelle runs away from a lion
options.why: The gazelle is escaping danger. The movement doesn’t help it locate a reproductive partner.

options.text: Foraging: a moth flies toward a female’s pheromones
options.why: The moth is locating a mate. Foraging involves movement used to obtain food.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes propulsion in a whale from propulsion in a typical fish?

options.text: The whale’s horizontal tail flukes move up and down
options.why: Vertical movement of the horizontal flukes provides thrust in whales. A typical fish’s tail moves mainly from side to side.

options.text: The whale’s forelimbs form gills that extract oxygen
options.why: The forelimbs form flippers used for control. Whales breathe air with lungs rather than extracting oxygen through gills.

options.text: The whale’s vertical tail fin moves from side to side
options.why: That arrangement describes a typical fish more closely. Whale flukes are horizontal and move up and down.

options.text: The whale’s hind limbs form paddles for forward thrust
options.why: Whales have greatly reduced external hind limbs. Their tail flukes provide the main propulsive force.
